g9-civics-uc4-t1.overview: Indigenous knowledge is the local knowledge a people builds over long histories of social life and interaction with the environment. This lesson defines it, shows why it differs from society to society, and surveys the rich indigenous knowledge systems of Ethiopia.
objectives: Define indigenous knowledge and explain its source
Explain why indigenous knowledge differs from society to society
List the types of indigenous knowledge practised in Ethiopian communities
Describe the practices of indigenous knowledge in your own community
Appreciate the value of local wisdom for solving local problems
g9-civics-uc4-t1.simple: Indigenous knowledge is knowledge developed by a local people over long histories of social life and interaction with their environment. It is based on the culture, traditions, social interactions, rituals, values and belief systems of a particular community, so it differs from society to society. It is passed down from elders to the young through practice, proverbs and stories. Ethiopia is rich in indigenous knowledge in architecture, pottery, traditional medicine, agriculture, cottage industry, conflict resolution and environmental conservation. For example, when a husband and wife quarrel, they often go to local elders who settle the matter through a win-win approach rather than to a court. Learning this knowledge helps us value local wisdom and use it to solve community problems.
g9-civics-uc4-t1.detailed:
What indigenous knowledge is. Indigenous knowledge is knowledge that has been developed by a local people as a result of long histories of their social life and interaction with their environment. It grows out of lived experience rather than a laboratory, and it is tested by generations of daily use. It is sometimes called local knowledge because it belongs to a particular place and a particular people.

Its foundation in culture. Indigenous knowledge is based on the culture, traditions, social interactions, rituals, values and belief systems of a particular community or society. Because cultures differ, indigenous knowledge is not the same from society to society. Each community builds the understanding it needs to survive and flourish in its own surroundings, and that understanding may not fit another community at all.

How it is transmitted. This knowledge is usually passed from elders to younger generations by word of mouth, by watching and doing, and through proverbs, songs, stories and rituals. Young people inherit the tradition because they are tomorrow's elders. The knowledge therefore stays alive only when each generation takes it up, practises it and hands it on again.

Ethiopia's rich heritage. Ethiopia is a country with rich indigenous knowledge systems in areas such as architecture, pottery, traditional medicine, agriculture, cottage industry, conflict resolution and environmental conservation. For instance, when a husband and a wife get into conflict they do not take the case immediately to a court; rather, they take it to local elders who resolve the disagreement through a win-win approach. This is a popular indigenous conflict resolution mechanism in most parts of Ethiopia.

Types of indigenous knowledge. Common types include traditional medicine, in which sick persons or domestic animals are treated with folk remedies; artisan crafts such as pottery, weaving, iron smithing, jewelry, wood carving and leather work; indigenous agriculture and soil and water conservation; indigenous conflict resolution; and indigenous environmental conservation. Each type carries practical skill, moral teaching and community memory at the same time.

Why the concept matters. Understanding the concept helps citizens see that useful knowledge does not come only from outside the country or from formal schooling. Local solutions are often cheap, accessible and well matched to the environment. Recognising indigenous knowledge also protects it from disappearing and builds pride in one's own culture and history.

keyTerms.def: Knowledge developed by a local people as a result of long histories of their social life and interaction with their environment.
The information, understanding and skills that a person gains through education or experience.
Locally organised mechanisms that work according to the custom and norms of a given society and the specific culture of a particular community.
The local knowledge and social taboos used to protect the environment and natural resources.
A set of actions performed in a fixed way by a community, which carries meaning, identity and shared values.
A way of settling a dispute in which both sides feel satisfied and no party is humiliated or defeated.
The treatment of sick persons or domestic animals with remedies prepared from local plants, minerals and other materials.
Small-scale local production carried out at home or in a workshop, such as pottery, weaving and leather work.

workedExamples.problem: A husband and wife in a rural kebele have a serious quarrel. Their neighbours could take them to the woreda court, but the elders are invited first. Which type of knowledge is being used and why is it preferred?
workedExamples.given: The conflict is between spouses; local elders are asked to settle it before any court is involved.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: indigenous conflict resolution is a locally organised mechanism working according to the custom and norms of a given society.
workedExamples.substitution: The elders apply the community's own custom rather than formal legal procedure.
workedExamples.calculation: Because the elders use a win-win approach, both sides accept the settlement and the relationship is repaired.
workedExamples.answer: Indigenous conflict resolution knowledge; it is preferred because it is peaceful, cheap and preserves relationships.

workedExamples.problem: A farmer treats his sick ox with a remedy prepared from local herbs instead of travelling to a distant veterinary clinic. Analyse this practice as indigenous knowledge.
workedExamples.given: The animal is sick; the farmer uses local plant remedies known in his community.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: indigenous knowledge is based on the values and belief systems of a community and grows from long interaction with the environment.
workedExamples.substitution: The remedy has been tested by generations of herders in that area.
workedExamples.calculation: The practice matches the definition of traditional medicine, which is one type of indigenous knowledge.
workedExamples.answer: It is traditional medicine, a clear example of indigenous knowledge developed through local experience.

workedExamples.problem: Two students argue about whether only knowledge learned in school counts as real knowledge. Using the concept of indigenous knowledge, decide who is right.
workedExamples.given: One student says only formal schooling produces knowledge; the other points to community knowledge.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: knowledge is the information, understanding and skills gained through education or experience.
workedExamples.substitution: Indigenous knowledge is gained through long experience of social life and the environment.
workedExamples.calculation: Since experience is a recognised source of knowledge, community knowledge is real knowledge too.
workedExamples.answer: The second student is right; knowledge also comes from experience, including indigenous knowledge.

commonMistakes: Believing that indigenous knowledge is the same in every Ethiopian community.
Thinking that only knowledge taught in school or written in books is real knowledge.
Assuming indigenous knowledge is old-fashioned, useless or inferior to imported knowledge.
Treating local elders and their mediation as unimportant because there is a modern court.
Forgetting that indigenous knowledge is transmitted by practice, proverbs, songs and stories, not by written manuals.
Confusing indigenous knowledge with a single subject such as traditional medicine, when it covers many fields.
applications: Asking local elders in your kebele to describe how they settle disputes peacefully.
Visiting a potter, weaver or blacksmith and recording the steps of the craft.
Learning the names and uses of local medicinal plants from an experienced elder.
Taking part in a Debo group when neighbours harvest or build a house.
Collecting proverbs from your community that encourage cooperation, hard work and respect.
Writing a short report on an indigenous practice found in your area for a civics lesson.
g9-civics-uc4-t1.summary: Indigenous knowledge is knowledge developed by a local people through long histories of social life and interaction with the environment, based on their culture, traditions, rituals, values and beliefs. Because cultures differ, it is not the same from society to society, and it is passed from elders to the young by practice and word of mouth. Ethiopia is rich in such knowledge in architecture, pottery, medicine, agriculture, cottage industry, conflict resolution and environmental conservation.

g9-civics-uc4-t2.overview: Indigenous knowledge shapes people who take responsibility for their community and country. This lesson explains how local conflict resolution, indigenous technologies and environmental conservation produce responsible citizens.
objectives: Define a responsible citizen and describe the role of change agent
Explain how indigenous conflict resolution builds sustainable peace
Describe how indigenous technologies support socio-economic participation
Explain the role of indigenous knowledge in environmental conservation
Demonstrate the roles of indigenous knowledge practised in your community
g9-civics-uc4-t2.simple: A responsible citizen is a person who has the knowledge and commitment to contribute to the betterment of their own livelihood, their community and their country, and who acts as a change agent for peace and development. Indigenous knowledge helps produce such citizens. Indigenous conflict resolution mechanisms, such as Jaarsummaa among the Oromo, Shimglina and Erq among the Amhara, Yejoka among the Gurage, Mada'a and Mablo among the Afar, Gedana among the Sidama and the Guurt system of the Somali, settle disputes peacefully at very low cost. Indigenous technologies such as pottery, weaving, iron smithing and wood carving let citizens use affordable local products. Konso terracing and Gedeo agroforestry show environmental conservation. By respecting this wisdom, young people grow into responsible citizens.
g9-civics-uc4-t2.detailed:
Who a responsible citizen is. A responsible citizen is a person who has the knowledge and commitment regarding his or her contributions for the betterment of his or her livelihood, the community and the country. Responsible citizens have vital roles as change agents in ensuring sustainable peace and the socio-economic transformation of their community and their country. This is the kind of citizen that indigenous knowledge helps to form.

Indigenous conflict resolution and peace building. Indigenous conflict resolution mechanisms can play a great role in ensuring sustainable peace in a given community by using peaceful resolution of conflicts at a very low cost. In every community this culture of resolving conflicts has been widely practised. Examples include Jaarsummaa of the Oromo, Shimglina and Erq of the Amhara, Yejoka of the Gurage, Mada'a and Mablo of the Afar, Gedana of the Sidama and the Guurt system of the Somali.

Why elders matter. In Ethiopia, indigenous conflict resolution mechanisms have paramount significance compared with modern conflict resolution institutions such as the court in ensuring sustainable peace. In these mechanisms elders take the lion's share in safeguarding the political, social, cultural, economic and religious life of their people. Although elders discharge this moral responsibility as members of their community and citizens of the country, it does not mean the role is left only to them; young people inherit this tradition from elders because they are tomorrow's elders.

Participation in socio-economic activities. Making active participation in the socio-economic activities of a society is one of the responsibilities expected of citizens. One of the ways citizens can contribute to the socio-economic transformation of their societies is by introducing and using indigenous technologies. Indigenous technologies and practices are very important for Ethiopia, which highly depends on outside supplies. They enable citizens to use local products at reasonable cost and with better accessibility compared with pricey and scarce imported products.

Indigenous technologies at work. Pottery, iron smithing, jewelry, weaving, wood carving and leather work are major indigenous technologies that have been in use for a long time in different parts of Ethiopia. The people engaged in these works maintained this indigenous knowledge and kept it from endangerment or disappearance with great dedication, resisting deep-rooted negative societal attitudes towards them. This shows real determination, hard work and respect for their own indigenous wisdom, which are true attributes of responsible or good citizens.

Environmental conservation. Environmental conservation refers to the wise use of resources available in the natural environment. Its life-supporting importance means it seeks the attention of everyone, because the life of both human beings and animals depends on a well conserved and preserved environment. Indigenous knowledge plays a significant role here: the Konso people's indigenous knowledge of water and soil conservation through terracing, and the Gedeo community's indigenous agroforestry system, are good examples. The link between environment and culture imposes moral and social responsibility, or prohibition mechanisms, on members to conserve their natural environment and not to damage it.

keyTerms.def: A person who has the knowledge and commitment regarding his or her contributions for the betterment of his or her livelihood, the community and the country.
A person who actively brings about positive improvement in the community, for example by building peace and development.
Lasting peace that continues over time because conflicts are resolved peacefully and fairly.
Locally organised mechanisms working according to the custom and norms of a given society to settle disputes peacefully.
Tools, crafts and techniques developed locally over a long period, such as pottery, weaving, iron smithing, wood carving and leather work.
The wise use of the resources available in the natural environment so that they are protected and preserved.
A farming system that combines trees with crops, as practised by the Gedeo community, to protect soil and produce food.
The indigenous conflict resolution mechanism of the Oromo people, led by elders.

workedExamples.problem: Two families in a kebele quarrel over a boundary and one threatens to use force. Elders of the community, not a court, settle the case. Show how this produces responsible citizens and peace.
workedExamples.given: A violent dispute exists, and local elders use the community's own conflict resolution mechanism.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: indigenous conflict resolution ensures sustainable peace using peaceful resolution at very low cost.
workedExamples.substitution: Elders mediate, both sides accept the settlement, and no party is defeated.
workedExamples.calculation: Force is avoided, the dispute ends, and the community learns that peace is possible without violence.
workedExamples.answer: The mechanism produces sustainable peace and teaches citizens responsibility, so it forms responsible citizens.

workedExamples.problem: A young person opens a small workshop making and selling woven baskets instead of importing plastic containers. Analyse the value of this choice.
workedExamples.given: A local product replaces a scarce and costly imported product.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: citizens contribute to socio-economic transformation by introducing and using indigenous technologies.
workedExamples.substitution: The workshop uses a local craft, so the price is reasonable and the goods are accessible.
workedExamples.calculation: The choice creates income, serves the community and reduces dependence on outside supplies.
workedExamples.answer: It shows a responsible citizen actively participating in socio-economic development through indigenous technology.

workedExamples.problem: Farmers on a steep hillside build stone terraces to hold back soil and water, as the Konso do. Explain how this act expresses responsible citizenship.
workedExamples.given: The land is steep and loses soil and water; the farmers use an indigenous conservation method.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: indigenous knowledge plays a significant role in promoting environmental conservation, which is everyone's concern.
workedExamples.substitution: Terracing is the Konso people's indigenous knowledge of water and soil conservation.
workedExamples.calculation: The terraces protect the land that supports present and future families, so the farmers serve both self and community.
workedExamples.answer: It is responsible citizenship, because they conserve the environment on which all life depends.

commonMistakes: Thinking that only the police and courts can keep peace in a community.
Believing indigenous conflict resolution is inferior to modern courts in ensuring lasting peace.
Assuming elders alone are responsible for peace, while young people need take no part.
Looking down on producers of pottery, weaving and leather work while using their products.
Believing Ethiopia must depend on imported goods instead of using local products.
Treating environmental conservation as the government's task rather than a personal duty.
Thinking that responsible citizenship is only about paying taxes and obeying laws.
applications: Taking part in a community peace meeting led by elders in your kebele.
Buying locally made pottery, woven cloth or leather goods instead of imported substitutes.
Planting trees and protecting a hillside, stream or grazing area near your village.
Organising a school club that warns against damaging the local environment.
Learning an indigenous craft or skill and teaching it to younger students.
Writing a report on how a local conflict was resolved without going to court.
g9-civics-uc4-t2.summary: A responsible citizen is committed to improving personal livelihood, the community and the country, and acts as a change agent for peace and development. Indigenous conflict resolution mechanisms, such as Jaarsummaa, Shimglina and Erq, Yejoka, Mada'a and Mablo, Gedana and Guurt, ensure sustainable peace peacefully and cheaply. Indigenous technologies give citizens affordable local products, and indigenous conservation knowledge such as Konso terracing and Gedeo agroforestry protects the environment.

g9-civics-uc4-t3.overview: Indigenous social institutions are locally created associations built on mutual trust to solve community problems. This lesson examines Idir, Iqub, Debo or Jigie, Mahber or Senbete and Siinqee and the services they provide.
objectives: List the main indigenous social institutions in Ethiopia
Describe the role of Idir in burial and sudden risk
Explain how Iqub solves the financial problems of members
Explain the importance of Debo, Mahber, Senbete and Siinqee
g9-civics-uc4-t3.simple: Indigenous social institutions are institutions established locally by the voluntary cooperation or association of community members on the basis of mutual trust, mainly to support one another. In Ethiopia they include Idir, Iqub, Debo or Jigie, Mahber or Senbete and Siinqee. Idir provides mutual aid in burial matters and also helps members cope with sudden risks such as the death of livestock, fire, theft or illness, and it can give interest-free loans. Iqub collects a fixed amount of money regularly and pays it to members by lottery, solving financial problems that banks cannot easily reach. Debo or Jigie is labour sharing during ploughing, weeding, harvesting and house building. Mahber or Senbete brings members together to help one another and enjoy social events, and Siinqee protects the rights of women and keeps peace. These institutions solve community problems cheaply and build solidarity.
g9-civics-uc4-t3.detailed:
What an indigenous social institution is. An indigenous social institution refers to institutions established locally by the voluntary cooperation or association of the members of a given community based on their own mutual trust. They are established by local people mainly to support each other. In Ethiopia these institutions have significant contributions to the day-to-day life activities of society by providing different socio-economic services to their members and to other needy people in the community.

Siinqee. Siinqee is literally a stick, called Ulee, and it symbolises a socially endorsed set of rights exercised by women in the Oromo society. It is a special stick used to signify legally married women and to indicate women's respect and power in society. In the Oromo Gadaa system, Siinqee is a symbolic representation of married women's participation in political, economic, social, cultural and religious activities. It plays significant roles in protecting women's rights and ensuring gender equality through Siinqee solidarity. If a woman has a Siinqee she must be respected and nobody should fight with her. Siinqee women also raise their Siinqee to ask conflicting parties to stop fighting immediately and then mediate between them to prevent the adverse consequences of conflict.

Idir. Idir is an indigenous social institution voluntarily established by local people mainly for self-help and other social activities. It is established primarily to provide mutual aid in burial matters and also to address other community concerns. It is widely practised and well known among both rural and urban peoples. Members contribute money and goods in kind on a regular basis to be used during mourning. Idir also helps members cope with sudden risks such as the death of livestock like oxen, asset losses from fire or theft, and health problems; it serves members during ceremonies such as weddings by providing materials; and it acts as a credit institution by providing members with loans without interest.

Iqub. Similar to Idir, Iqub is an indigenous social institution voluntarily established by people on the basis of mutual trust, and its primary objective is providing financial services to members. Members agree to collect a specific amount of money on a regular basis by setting a specific date, perhaps per week or per month, and the pooled money is paid to members through a lottery method. Iqub therefore has a crucial role in solving the financial problems of members which cannot be accessed from formal financial institutions like banks and microfinance.

Mahber or Senbete. Mahber or Senbete are voluntary associations of individuals who help each other when a member faces a serious problem such as death or the burning down of property, who enjoy together and who take part in other social activities. Members gather at one common place per week or per month to discuss issues related to their common interests. In some cases members prepare food and drinks at their homes and serve the members, or bring the food and drinks to their religious place, enjoy it together and feed the poor gathered there. This institution is vital for individuals to get together, help each other and deal with the concerns of their community.

Debo or Jigie. Debo or Jigie refers to the culture of helping each other among local people during ploughing, weeding and other events such as harvesting and building houses. It has been widely known and practised in different areas of Ethiopia for a long time. For example, when unexpected rain comes during harvesting time, farmers harvest their crops in Debo or Jigie to save them from damage. The indigenous social institutions discussed here are not the only ones practised by all sections of society in Ethiopia; there are many other similar institutions that need to be promoted and given great emphasis by all concerned bodies.

keyTerms.def: An institution established locally by the voluntary cooperation or association of the members of a community, based on their own mutual trust, mainly to support one another.
An indigenous social institution voluntarily established by local people to provide mutual aid in burial matters and to address other community concerns.
An indigenous social institution voluntarily established by people on the basis of mutual trust to provide financial services to members.
The culture of helping one another among local people during ploughing, weeding, harvesting, house building and other activities.
Voluntary associations of individuals who help each other in serious problems, enjoy together and take part in social activities.
A stick, called Ulee, that symbolises a socially endorsed set of rights exercised by women in the Oromo society, signifying married women's respect and power.
The confidence members have in one another, on which indigenous social institutions are built.
The Oromo indigenous social and political system in which Siinqee symbolises married women's participation in public life.

workedExamples.problem: A family in a town loses its income because the father dies. Members of the community raise money and goods for the funeral and later offer an interest-free loan. Which institution is at work and what services does it give?
workedExamples.given: The family faces a burial and a sudden loss; members contribute money and goods regularly.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: Idir is voluntarily established mainly to provide mutual aid in burial matters and to address other community concerns.
workedExamples.substitution: The contribution for mourning plus the interest-free loan matches the services of Idir.
workedExamples.calculation: Idir covers burial costs, helps cope with sudden risks, and acts as a credit institution without interest.
workedExamples.answer: Idir. It provides burial support, helps with sudden risks and gives interest-free loans.

workedExamples.problem: A market woman cannot get a bank loan because she has no collateral. She and twenty others agree to contribute a fixed sum each month and to give the whole amount to one member by lottery. Identify and explain the institution.
workedExamples.given: A group pools a fixed monthly amount and pays it out to one member at a time by lottery.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: Iqub provides financial services by collecting a specific amount regularly and paying it to members by lottery.
workedExamples.substitution: The group meets the definition exactly, with a set date and a lottery method.
workedExamples.calculation: Each member receives a lump sum in turn, so money becomes available without bank collateral.
workedExamples.answer: Iqub, which solves financial problems that formal institutions such as banks cannot easily reach.

workedExamples.problem: Rain threatens a farmer's ripening crop and there is too much work for one household. Neighbours arrive to harvest together and the crop is saved. Which institution is this and what value does it teach?
workedExamples.given: Neighbours share labour at a critical moment to save crops from damage.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: Debo or Jigie is the culture of helping each other during ploughing, weeding, harvesting and house building.
workedExamples.substitution: The shared harvesting matches the Debo or Jigie practice described in the lesson.
workedExamples.calculation: The work is finished in time, the crop is saved and cooperation is strengthened.
workedExamples.answer: Debo or Jigie, which teaches cooperation, mutual support and the value of labour sharing.

workedExamples.problem: A husband beats his wife and relatives are about to fight. Married women raise a special stick and demand that the fighting stop, then mediate. Explain this institution and its importance.
workedExamples.given: Conflicting parties are separated by women holding a symbolic stick and are then mediated.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: Siinqee symbolises a socially endorsed set of rights held by women in the Oromo society and protects women's rights and peace.
workedExamples.substitution: The raised Siinqee signals that the woman must be respected and that fighting must end at once.
workedExamples.calculation: The conflict is stopped before it causes further harm and the parties are reconciled.
workedExamples.answer: Siinqee; it protects women's rights, promotes gender equality and helps ensure peace and conflict resolution.

commonMistakes: Thinking indigenous social institutions exist only in rural areas and not in towns.
Believing Idir is only about burial and nothing else, when it also copes with sudden risks and gives interest-free loans.
Confusing Iqub with a bank, and thinking it charges interest like a formal lender.
Assuming Debo or Jigie is a religious ceremony rather than a system of labour sharing.
Treating Siinqee as an ordinary walking stick instead of a symbol of women's rights.
Thinking Mahber or Senbete is only for eating and drinking, ignoring its mutual aid role.
Believing that only the government can solve community problems.
applications: Joining your family in paying its regular Idir contribution in the kebele.
Starting or joining a small Iqub saving group with classmates or neighbours.
Helping a neighbour with harvesting, weeding or house building in a Debo group.
Taking part in a Mahber or Senbete gathering that also feeds the poor.
Respecting women's rights, as symbolised by Siinqee, in school and at home.
Interviewing elders about an institution in your community not covered in the lesson and reporting to class.
g9-civics-uc4-t3.summary: Indigenous social institutions are established locally through the voluntary cooperation of community members on the basis of mutual trust, mainly to support one another. In Ethiopia they include Idir, Iqub, Debo or Jigie, Mahber or Senbete and Siinqee. Idir provides burial aid, helps with sudden risks and gives interest-free loans; Iqub provides rotating financial services; Debo or Jigie shares labour; Mahber or Senbete combines mutual help with social gathering; and Siinqee protects women's rights and peace.

by a private company for profit

questions.explanation: Idir helps members cope with sudden risks such as the death of livestock, fire, theft and health problems.

questions.q: Explain the main purpose of Mahber or Senbete.
questions.answer: to help each other in serious problems and enjoy and socialise together|mutual help and social gatherings
questions.explanation: Members help each other in serious problems, enjoy together and discuss common interests.

questions.q: In which Oromo system does Siinqee symbolise married women's participation in public life?
questions.explanation: In the Oromo Gadaa system Siinqee represents married women's participation in political, economic, social, cultural and religious activities.

questions.q: Arrange the steps of an Iqub meeting in the correct order.
options: The winner receives the pooled money
Members agree on the amount and the date
Members contribute their money on the set date
The winner is chosen by lottery
questions.explanation: First the group agrees on the amount and date, then members contribute, then the winner is drawn by lottery, then the money is paid.
